title: DIKW Hierarchy
body:
The **DIKW hierarchy** separates four levels that arguments about data routinely conflate.

```
Data          raw values with no context              37.2
Information   data with context, answering what        a temperature of 37.2°C
Knowledge     patterns across information, answering how   this patient's fever is falling
Wisdom        judgement about what should be done      whether to discharge them
```

Each level requires the one below it and none is produced automatically by having more of it.
That is the reason the hierarchy earns its place in this course: a system collecting enormous
quantities of data has produced data, and the claim that it therefore possesses knowledge skips
two levels that require interpretation and judgement.

Most overstated claims about a dataset are a level confusion. A model that finds a correlation
has produced information, and treating it as knowledge requires a mechanism, which
[[Correlation]] in [[STATISTICS]] warns about directly. Treating it as wisdom requires a value
judgement about what to do, which no dataset contains.

The hierarchy also explains why the top level resists automation most. Deciding what should be
done depends on which outcomes matter, and that is the question [[Ethical Analysis]]
answers and no computation reaches.
